routes.description: Establish Jesus's death, the empty tomb, and sincere postmortem appearance claims, then argue that bodily resurrection provides the best cumulative explanation of those historical facts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal facts are historically warranted, their earliest interpretation is bodily, and resurrection explains them more adequately than rescue, survival, visionary, or developmental alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative best-explanation inference to the conclusion that Jesus physically rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Roman crucifixion resulted in Jesus's physical death.
Establish that Jesus was buried and that his body was subsequently absent from the tomb.
Establish sincere postmortem appearance claims involving disciples, Paul, and James.
Show that bodily resurrection explains the combined facts better than the competing accounts presented.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that early creedal and Pauline resurrection language referred to bodily raising rather than only spiritual vindication.
Account for apparent source differences without treating the physical resurrection tradition as a later invention.

routes.description: Contest the death, empty-tomb, and physical-appearance premises while showing that early belief and later narrative development permit survival, rescue, visionary, spiritual-vindication, or underdetermined accounts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a necessary premise remains historically uncertain or if the evidence does not discriminate sufficiently between bodily resurrection and the available nonresurrection interpretations.

motionBridge.description: Connect uncertainty in the premises or inference to the conclusion that physical resurrection is not historically established.

centralBridges.description: Show that the sources do not establish irreversible physical death on the cross with the certainty required by the resurrection inference.
Show that early resurrection and appearance claims need not describe encounters with Jesus's physically revived body.
Show that increasingly explicit physical details can be explained by narrative or theological development.
Demonstrate that rescue, survival, visionary experience, spiritual vindication, or uncertainty remain coherent alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the affirmative inference to establish its exceptional conclusion without assuming the theological vindication it seeks to prove.
Distinguish early Pauline and creedal material from later tomb and appearance narratives when assessing bodily content.

sections.title: Historical Burden and Best-Explanation Method
sections.rationale: Defines what the affirmative must establish, how cumulative explanatory comparison operates, and whether uncertainty or a coherent alternative is sufficient to defeat the motion.

sections.title: Death by Crucifixion
sections.rationale: Addresses the necessary premise that Jesus irreversibly died, including Roman practice, the duration and details of crucifixion, Pilate's conduct, and proposed survival or rescue interpretations.

sections.title: Burial and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Tests whether bodily absence from a known burial place is historically established and whether early resurrection belief required the original body to leave a tomb.

sections.title: Appearances and Bodily Physicality
sections.rationale: Examines what the disciples, Paul, and James reportedly experienced and whether sincere appearance claims establish encounters with a physically resurrected Jesus rather than visions or spiritual vindication.

sections.title: Early Tradition and Narrative Development
sections.rationale: Evaluates the dating and bodily meaning of creedal and Pauline material, source relationships, Gospel differences, and the claim that explicit physical details intensified over time.

chunk-001:c001.proposition: Multiple historical sources, the lethal character of Roman crucifixion and its preceding torture, and medical opinion support the conclusion that Jesus died by crucifixion.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: The Jerusalem setting of the burial and resurrection proclamation, the opponents' stolen-body explanation, and the bodily meaning of resurrection support an empty tomb.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: The disciples and former foes Paul and James sincerely believed that the risen Jesus appeared to them, contributing to a cumulative resurrection explanation of the death, empty tomb, and appearances.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Creedal material predating Paul and Paul's resurrection language indicate that the earliest tradition concerned the raising, transformation, and appearance of Jesus's body.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: An early creed, repeated Pauline death-and-resurrection language, and shared apostolic preaching trace belief in Jesus's death and bodily resurrection to the original disciples.

chunk-002:c002-05.proposition: The rescue theory lacks early evidence, conflicts with the asserted eyewitness testimony, depends on a source written centuries later, and is ad hoc as an explanation of the historical evidence.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: A survival theory cannot securely rely on Pilate's desire to save Jesus because that detail is less historically well attested than Jesus's death by crucifixion.

chunk-003:c003-06.proposition: Bodily resurrection explains the asserted death, empty tomb, and appearance facts, whereas the rescue theory lacks evidence, strains the sources, conflicts with eyewitness testimony, and is ad hoc.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: The historical evidence does not establish either Jesus's death on the cross or later encounters with him in physical bodily form, leaving two necessary premises of the bodily-resurrection inference unproved.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: An early belief that Jesus was alive with God could express spiritual vindication and therefore does not itself entail bodily revival or discovery of an empty tomb.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: Paul includes his own spiritually described appearance in the same list as the earlier appearances, weakening the inference that those earlier reports necessarily concerned physical encounters with Jesus's body.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: The earliest Gospel evidence does not firmly establish death on the cross because Mark depicts an unusually short crucifixion and Pilate's doubt, while the decisive spear wound appears only in the later Gospel of John.

chunk-002:c002-03.proposition: John's piercing, unbroken-leg, and related crucifixion details may reflect scriptural and theological construction rather than independent eyewitness evidence establishing the manner and certainty of Jesus's death.

chunk-002:c002-04.proposition: The increasingly severe and explicit crucifixion details across the Gospels indicate narrative evolution, so later physical detail need not preserve eyewitness testimony about Jesus's death and resurrection.

chunk-002:c002-09.proposition: Paul's luminous experience and James's later leadership do not establish that either man encountered Jesus physically, so their conversions or prominence do not prove a bodily resurrection.

chunk-003:c003-01.proposition: The sealed-tomb objection to survival combines later empty-tomb traditions with earlier evidence that neither reports an empty tomb nor requires the original body to leave its burial place.

chunk-003:c003-04.proposition: A bodily-resurrection claimant bears the burden of proof, and delayed, selective, increasingly physical New Testament reports do not establish that the earliest resurrection proclamation described a bodily event.

chunk-003:c003-08.proposition: The earliest resurrection proclamation required neither an empty tomb nor a physical body, while the later Gospels progressively physicalized the appearances and amplified the account of Jesus's death.
